title: Dismas, the good thief (25 March)
hook: the man crucified beside Jesus, honored by tradition as a saint

segments.voice: Yesterday, Turibius of Mongrovejo, the archbishop of Lima who crossed his diocese on foot and by mule. Your line was he walked it all. Who did you go and see? Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

Three crosses on a hill outside Jerusalem. Crucifixion is how Rome punishes rebels and criminals in public. In the middle hangs Jesus. On either side, a man the Gospel of Luke calls a malefactor, an evildoer. One of them joins the crowd's mockery: if you're the Christ, save yourself, and us. The other one tells him to stop. And then, in a few short words, he asks for something. Today, a dying thief's request, and the man the Church remembers as Dismas.

Start with what the text actually gives us, because it's very little. Luke doesn't name him. Matthew and Mark simply call the two men thieves, and they say both of them reviled Jesus. Luke alone tells it differently: one mocks, and the other rebukes him. We are getting what we deserve, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then he speaks to Jesus. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom." Notice what he doesn't ask. Not to be taken down. Not to be spared. Just to be remembered. And the answer comes back at once: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." The name Dismas comes later, from an old writing outside the Bible, sometimes called the Gospel of Nicodemus; the Church doesn't treat it as scripture, but the name stuck, and tradition honors him as a saint. Catholics have read this scene in more than one way. Some see in it how wide mercy is: a man with nothing to show, at the very end, hears the word paradise. Others notice his honesty first: he names his own guilt plainly before he asks for anything. And some notice a quieter thing. On a hill where people mock, he is the one who speaks to Jesus as a king. A thief's last request has become a prayer. Some Catholics say it at the end of the day, or at a deathbed. A short prayer, from the worst possible place, and an answer for this very day.
screen: `LUKE ALONE TELLS IT THIS WAY.` · `HE ASKS ONLY TO BE REMEMBERED.` · `THE NAME COMES FROM LATER TRADITION.` · `MERCY, HONESTY, A KING ON A CROSS.` · then, large: `LORD, REMEMBER ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the people in prison. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people behind bars, near you or far away. Someone you know, maybe, or someone you've only read about. Someone waiting for trial. Someone who will never get out. Someone who is guilty and knows it, like the man on the cross. Don't sort them into deserving and undeserving. Just hold them. If you pray, you can pray the thief's own words for them: Lord, remember me, remember them. If you don't, simply let them be remembered by you. The bell holds the time.
Dismas. The name tradition gives the man crucified beside Jesus, who asked only to be remembered, and was promised paradise.
Your line: remember me. Today, find out one thing about a prison or jail near you, or about someone in it. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: The good thief is remembered on 25 March in some places; Catholics often pray for prisoners and those who are dying with his words, and some prison ministries take him as their patron.
